title: The Signs of the Art: Planets, Zodiac, Elements and Alchemical Characters
family: Not an alphabet. The shorthand signs (notae) of astronomy, astrology and alchemy, with the sixteen dot figures of geomancy. They stand for things, not sounds.
summary: Not an alphabet but the shorthand of the heavens and the laboratory. In Alexander Jones's reading of the Roman-period astronomical papyri from Oxyrhynchus, the planet signs began as abbreviations of the planets' Greek names. The zodiac and alchemical signs are attested chiefly in medieval Greek and Latin manuscripts, and early modern printed tables standardised them. Agrippa treats the 'seals and characters' that the stars stamp on natural things (De occulta philosophia I.33), and the sixteen geomantic figures with the characters drawn from them (II.48, II.51). Unicode encoded the planet and zodiac signs in version 1.1 (1993) and an Alchemical Symbols block in 6.0 (2010). The geomantic figures are not encoded as of Unicode 15.0.

firstAttestation.work: Astronomical tables, almanacs and horoscopes on papyrus from Oxyrhynchus, published as P. Oxy. 4133-4300a
firstAttestation.author: anonymous scribes and astronomers; edited by Alexander Jones (1999)
firstAttestation.date: Roman period. The collection runs from about the 1st to the 5th century CE; I could not check which dated papyrus carries the earliest sign.
firstAttestation.locator: A. Jones, Astronomical Papyri from Oxyrhynchus, vol. 1, introduction, on the symbols and abbreviations used in the papyri (page not verified).
firstAttestation.notes: This is the earliest attestation I can name, and only for the PLANET signs. It rests on Jones's edition as I recall it and as secondary summaries report it, not on any papyrus seen in this run. The zodiac glyphs are not attested this early in any source named here: the Greek horoscopes collected by Neugebauer and Van Hoesen usually write the sign names out or abbreviate them (recalled). For the ALCHEMICAL signs the earliest witnesses named here are the lists of signs in Byzantine manuscripts of the Greek alchemical corpus, chief among them Marcianus graecus 299 (10th or 11th century), printed by Berthelot (1887). The element triangles and most of the Unicode alchemical repertoire are attested here only from 17th- and 18th-century printed tables. Basis: recalled, not re-checked (web search was exhausted in this run).

claims.claim: The planet signs began as abbreviations of the planets' Greek names in Roman-period astronomical papyri.
claims.evidence: Jones's edition of the Oxyrhynchus astronomical papyri (1999) is the basis usually cited. Basis: recalled, not re-checked (web search was exhausted in this run).

claims.claim: Saturn's sign comes from κρ (Κρόνος), Jupiter's from ζ (Ζεύς), Mars's from Θοῦρος, Venus's from Φωσφόρος, Mercury's from Στίλβων.
claims.evidence: This is the letter-by-letter reading reported from Jones. Earlier writers, Maunder (1934) among them, explained the signs as pictures of the gods' attributes. I could not check how firmly Jones commits to each letter. Present them as Jones's readings. Basis: recalled, not re-checked (web search was exhausted in this run).

claims.claim: The signs picture the gods' attributes: Saturn's sickle, Jupiter's thunderbolt, Mars's shield and spear, Venus's hand-mirror, Mercury's caduceus.
claims.evidence: A very old and still popular reading. It explains the later shapes but not, on Jones's evidence, their origin. Report it as a reading. Basis: recalled, not re-checked (web search was exhausted in this run).

claims.claim: The crosses at the foot of Mercury and Venus, and on Saturn and Jupiter, are late additions to the signs.
claims.evidence: Secondary summaries say the crosses are not in the papyrus forms and became standard in late medieval and Renaissance copies. Not checked against plates. Do not say they were added 'to Christianise' the signs without a source. Basis: recalled, not re-checked (web search was exhausted in this run).

claims.claim: The zodiac glyphs are as old as the planet signs.
claims.evidence: In the Greek horoscopes collected by Neugebauer and Van Hoesen (1959) the signs are usually written out or abbreviated (recalled). The pictorial glyphs are a feature of medieval manuscripts. Proposed derivations such as Capricorn from τρ (τράγος) and Virgo from ΠΑΡ (Παρθένος) are unproven. Basis: recalled, not re-checked (web search was exhausted in this run).

claims.claim: Before late antiquity the pairing of metals and planets was not fixed.
claims.evidence: Celsus's Mithraic ladder in Origen, Contra Celsum VI.22, gives tin to Aphrodite, bronze to Zeus and iron to Hermes. A list ascribed to Olympiodorus gives electrum to Zeus and tin to Hermes. The later standard is lead-Saturn, tin-Jupiter, iron-Mars, gold-Sun, copper-Venus, quicksilver-Mercury, silver-Moon. Basis: recalled, not re-checked (web search was exhausted in this run).
sources: Origen, Contra Celsum VI.22, trans. Chadwick 1953

claims.claim: Byzantine manuscripts of Greek alchemy carry lists of signs for metals, minerals and operations, the metals written with planet signs.
claims.evidence: Marcianus graecus 299 (10th or 11th c.) and Parisinus graecus 2327 (1478); lists printed by Berthelot (1887). Folios not verified. Basis: recalled, not re-checked (web search was exhausted in this run).

claims.claim: Alchemical signs were a secret code.
claims.evidence: They were mostly abbreviations, used in recipes, notebooks and pharmacy as the planet signs were in tables. Alchemical secrecy relied more on cover-names (Decknamen) than on the signs (Principe 2013). Some authors did use signs to hide matter from casual readers. Basis: recalled, not re-checked (web search was exhausted in this run).

claims.claim: The four element triangles are ancient.
claims.evidence: I can name no ancient or medieval source for them. They are standard in 17th- and 18th-century printed tables (e.g. Sommerhoff 1701). Their reading as halves of a hexagram cannot be dated here. Basis: recalled, not re-checked (web search was exhausted in this run).

letters.name: Sun

letters.form: One open circle, centre (50,50), radius 38. One solid dot at the centre, radius 6. Nothing else.

letters.name: Capricorn

letters.form: Begin at the top left with a small hook at (12,20); the stroke drops as an upright at x=24 to its foot at (24,90). letters.name: Via (the Way)
letters.value: geomantic figure; planet: Moon (Agrippa, De occulta philosophia II.48, as recalled)
letters.translit: no Unicode code point (none as of Unicode 15.0)
letters.form: Four rows of solid dots, radius 6, read from top to bottom. head row (y=14): ONE dot at x=50; neck row (y=38): ONE dot at x=50; body row (y=62): ONE dot at x=50; feet row (y=86): ONE dot at x=50. Pattern 1-1-1-1 (1 = one dot, 2 = two dots). 4 dots in all.
letters.note: The dot pattern is the same in every Latin geomancy (Charmasson 1980; Skinner 1980), so the drawing is safe. Manuscripts write the points as dots, small circles or short strokes; I have not seen how the 1533 Agrippa prints them. The planet follows the Latin tradition that Agrippa repeats in II.48 (recalled). Zodiac attributions are deliberately NOT given: they differ between Agrippa, the geomancy ascribed to Gerard of Cremona and later sources. In II.51 Agrippa derives line-characters from each figure by joining its points; those characters are NOT described here and must be traced from the 1533 plate.
letters.earliestForm: The sixteen figures reach Latin from Arabic ʿilm al-raml in the 12th century (Hugh of Santalla; Charmasson 1980). The Latin names given here are those of the medieval Latin tradition. Basis: recalled, not re-checked (web search was exhausted in this run).

lettersSource: Not an alphabet. The 'letters' are the 51 units the page will show. Nos. 1-35 are Unicode-encoded signs: 7 planets, 12 zodiac signs, 4 elements, 3 principles (Mercury shares its sign with the planet), 5 substances (antimony, vitriol, sal ammoniac, aqua fortis, aqua regia) and 4 operations (sublimation, precipitation, distillation, putrefaction). Nos. 36-51 are the 16 geomantic figures, which have no code point as of Unicode 15.0. Each 'form' describes the MODERN STANDARD shape, read off Noto Sans Symbols (@fontsource/noto-sans-symbols 5.3.0, rendered and examined on a 10 x 10 grid in this session) on a 100-unit box, y downward. It is not traced from Agrippa, from a manuscript or from the papyri. 'earliestForm' says what is known of the earliest shape; most of it is recalled and unverified, so no 'earliest form' variant should be drawn. The geomantic figures follow the standard dot patterns of Latin geomancy (Charmasson 1980; Skinner 1980), not Agrippa's 1533 plate, which was not seen. Each letter carries extra fields: group, codepoint, char, unicodeName, earliestForm, earliestConfidence (and rows for the geomantic figures, top to bottom).

links.relation: The planet signs began as abbreviations of the planets' Greek names (Κρόνος, Ζεύς, Θοῦρος, Φωσφόρος, Στίλβων), on Jones's reading.
Same world: the astronomical papyri that carry the earliest planet signs come from Greek-writing Roman Egypt, where astrology and magic shared scribes and vocabulary.
Agrippa's Latin chapters on characters (I.33, II.48, II.51, II.52), the Latin geomantic names, and the Paracelsian tria prima.
Geomancy comes from Arabic ʿilm al-raml; Arabic alchemy carried the Greek signs and theory into Latin.
The Syriac alchemical corpus (Berthelot and Duval, 1893) is a bridge between Greek and Arabic alchemy.
Agrippa's 'characters of things' (I.33) and the characters drawn from geomantic figures (II.51) belong to the long practice of magical characters.
The planetary seals of II.22 are a different set of signs from the planet signs shown here; do not confuse them.
Book III's angelic alphabets (III.29-30) are Agrippa's other kind of character; this page covers the signs of things, not of letters.

Unicode calls Venus FEMALE SIGN and Mars MALE SIGN, and spells Scorpio SCORPIUS. Use the planet and sign names on the page.
U+2648-U+2653 (zodiac) render as coloured emoji on most phones. Draw them as SVG, or add U+FE0E after each.
U+1F71A GOLD and U+1F71B SILVER have unusual reference glyphs (a flourished sun; a ring with three small rings in Noto). Use the Sun and Moon signs for gold and silver, as the alchemists did.
U+1F70F BLACK SULFUR is the sign popularly called the "Leviathan cross", used today by a living organisation as an emblem. It is not shown here; if mentioned, do not reproduce it as an emblem.
Uranus, Neptune and Pluto (U+2645-U+2647) are modern signs and outside this page.
